OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane published an essay on 4 November 2026 urging politicians to shape AI policy ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
He compares AI’s economic impact to the New Deal and calls for a "compelling third path" that lets citizens share AI benefits.
Lehane lists five policy priorities covering worker protections, education, safety and data‑center development.

Lehane’s essay follows a Democratic midterm win that flipped Congress amid voter frustration over cost of living, a context that amplifies concerns about AI‑driven job loss and data‑center electricity use.
Kate Brennan of the AI Now Institute noted the shift from OpenAI’s prior focus on accelerating development to advocating broader adoption and infrastructure support.
The proposals aim to expand AI use while addressing economic disruption, though critics say the New Deal analogy may serve OpenAI’s own interests.

entries.text: The same day, the company’s chief policy officer, Irene Solaiman, discussed the commercial and risk implications of open‑source AI in a TechCrunch Equity podcast released 4 November 2026.
The conversation highlighted how enterprises and governments are adopting open models to reduce costs while weighing security and value‑capture concerns.
Kimi‑K3.1‑Pro is a 2.8‑trillion‑parameter mixture‑of‑experts model with a 1‑million‑token context window and 104 billion activated parameters per inference.
It uses a hybrid attention design combining KDA and gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention to handle long contexts efficiently.

Solaiman explained that open models lower licensing fees but shift expenses to infrastructure, data curation, and compliance, and that companies must assess trade‑offs between model size, performance, and operational risk.

Amazon Bedrock introduced AgentCore Evaluations, a feature that can score AI agents throughout their lifecycle using decision models that return calibrated probabilities instead of free‑form text.
The capability supports both built‑in evaluators and custom ones that you define as either an LLM‑as‑a‑judge or a code‑based evaluator running in AWS Lambda.
By November 4, 2026 the service allowed users to connect external decision‑model backends such as Jev and Strands Decider 2B through code‑based evaluators.
Decision models answer fixed‑answer questions like whether a response stayed on policy or matched retrieved context, providing a label and a numeric score that can be thresholded for trust.

Custom LLM‑as‑a‑judge evaluators apply user‑provided instructions and rating scales, while code‑based evaluators can invoke any external system, model, or API, including hosted models like Jev from TypeSafe or the open‑source Strands Decider 2B that users run themselves.

The design lets multiple questions be answered in a single request, enabling a screening layer that flags turns for deeper analysis by built‑in evaluators, which also supply explanations for debugging.
Traditional agent evaluation relies on free‑form text outputs whose confidence can drift, making automated scoring difficult for compliance and safety checks.
Decision models, which output a probability over a predefined set of answers, offer a more stable metric for policy enforcement and harmfulness detection.
This approach aligns with broader industry moves toward structured evaluation to maintain auditability and reduce manual review effort.

The UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan told parliament that AI could add between £55 billion and £140 billion to the economy by 2030, with a central estimate of £120 billion, after admitting the earlier £400 billion claim was overstated.
The earlier figure had been used by government departments for almost two years despite being based on a Google‑commissioned report.
Narayan said the new estimate remains highly uncertain.
The £400 billion number came from a 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First (now PF Global) and was promoted by the government to allay fears of job losses.
PF Global’s head of economics Jonathan Dupont explained the gap as a result of the government assuming a slower AI adoption rate than the 2023 model projected.
Skills England continued to cite the £400 billion figure four months after the minister’s admission, showing lag in updating public communications.
The minister’s revised range of £55‑£140 billion reflects a more modest but still significant contribution of AI and data investment to the UK economy.
Economic impact estimates for AI are often based on models that assume how quickly businesses adopt the technology and how much data they invest in.
problems: model check: Source mentions model assumptions about adoption speed but does not mention assumptions about data‑investment levels.
